# What this is about

We are building an open database of protest events in Germany.
A pipeline collects articles from around 74 German news outlets, keeps those that
mention *Protest* or *Demonstration*, downloads the full text, and then has a
**locally running language model** read each article and fill in a structured set
of variables (where, when, who, how many, what about, what happened).
The result feeds a public dashboard for researchers, journalists and the public.

That is all you need to know about the project. What matters for your work is the
next paragraph.

## Why we need you

We do not know how good the machine annotation actually is. To find out, we need a
**gold standard**: the same articles, coded carefully by humans. Your annotations
are that gold standard. We compare them against the machine output to estimate
precision and recall for every variable, and we compare coders against each other
to check that the coding scheme itself is reliable.

This has three consequences for how you should work:

* **Code independently.** Do not discuss individual articles with other coders
  while you are coding them. If a *general* rule is unclear, ask the project lead —
  the answer will be shared with everyone.
* **Do not guess what the machine would say.** You are not correcting the model,
  you are coding the article. You will never see the model's output.
* **Consistency beats speed.** A field that is filled in the same way by everyone
  is worth more than a field that is filled in quickly.

::: {.callout-important}
The sample was drawn with a **keyword filter**. Many articles mention "Protest" or
"Demonstration" without describing a protest event at all. In the pilot round,
roughly **half** of all articles contained no protest. Coding an article as "no
protest" is a real and valuable result, not a failure to find something.
:::

# What you will do

The project contains **250 news articles**. For each article you:

1. decide whether it describes at least one protest event;
2. if it does, describe each protest event using the form on the right-hand side
   of the screen;
3. submit and move on to the next article.

An article with no protest takes well under a minute. A long article about a
nationwide day of action with several crowd estimates can take fifteen. Both are
normal.

Unless you are told otherwise, work through the articles in the order Label Studio
presents them, and do not skip ahead — all coders start at the top of the same
queue so that our articles overlap.

# Getting started

## Access

<!-- Server address and invitation link are inserted here. -->

*The server address and your personal invitation link are given separately.*

Open the link in a normal browser (Firefox or Chrome), create an account with your
work e-mail address and pick a password. You will land on the project overview.

## Opening the annotation job

You should see a single project called **`protest_validation`**. Do **not** click
on the project name itself — that opens the data browser. Instead:

1. click the **`...`** menu at the right edge of the project card;
2. choose **Label**.

![Opening the annotation job from the project overview](select.png){width=6in}

The two numbers under the project name (`11 / 250` in the screenshot) show how many
articles have been annotated in total, by everybody.

## The annotation screen

![The annotation interface. Left: the article. Right: the form.](label.png){width=6.5in}

The screen has two halves:

**Left — the article.** Headline, publication date, and the full article text.
This is everything you are allowed to use. Very long articles (live tickers, for
example) are cut off after 20,000 characters, so a text may end mid-sentence.
Code what is in front of you and mention the truncation in the notes if it matters.

**Right — the form.** At first you only see *Step 1* and the *Annotator Notes*
box. As soon as you answer Step 1 with "Yes / Possibly", the form for **Protest 1**
appears below it. Further protest blocks appear only when you ask for them
(see @sec-more).

**Bottom bar.** Left to right: the article ID and your position in the queue
(`12 of 12`), arrows to move between articles, undo / redo / reset for the current
form, and the **Skip** and **Submit** buttons.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The single most common mistake

Free-text boxes are **not** saved by simply typing in them. After typing you must
press **Shift + Enter** or click the **Add** button next to the box. The text then
appears as a small entry underneath the box. If you type and hit *Submit*
straight away, **the text is lost**.

Checkboxes and radio buttons do not have this problem — they are stored as soon as
you click them.
:::

## Saving, skipping, stopping

* **Submit** stores the annotation for the current article and loads the next one.
  There is no separate save button — everything is stored per article on submit.
* You can stop at any time and continue later. Submitted articles stay submitted.
* Use the arrows at the bottom left to go back to an article you have already
  submitted; change what you need and submit again.
* **Skip** only for technically broken articles: empty text, a paywall stub with
  two sentences of teaser, an error page, or a text in a language you cannot read.
  Write one line in the notes before skipping.
* Do **not** use Skip for articles that simply contain no protest. Those get
  `has_protest = no` and a Submit.

# The rules that apply everywhere {#sec-rules}

These seven rules resolve most of the questions that come up.

1. **Only the article counts.** Code what this text says. Do not use your own
   knowledge about the event, do not look it up. If the article does not say how 
   many people came, we do not know how many people came. Geographical common 
   knowledge is the one exception: you may fill in that Köln is in 
   Nordrhein-Westfalen.

2. **Answer every yes/no question.** A blank field is not the same as "No" — for
   us it is missing data and it damages the statistics. Every coloured yes/no block
   in the form must have an answer before you submit.

3. **"No" means "the article does not report it."** For counter-protestors,
   arrests, protester violence, property damage, injuries and deaths, tick **No**
   both when the article states that it did not happen *and* when the article is
   silent about it. **Police is the only exception**: it has a separate
   *Not reported* option.

4. **Do not infer, do not embellish.** "Die Polizei war im Einsatz" does not tell
   you that there were arrests. A demonstration organized by a trade union does
   not tell you that the participants were trade union members.

5. **Write content fields in German**, close to the wording of the article. The
   form labels are English, the content is not. `main_issue`, `target`, slogans,
   organizations, demographics and keywords are German.

6. **Quotes are verbatim.** Where a field asks for a citation, copy and paste from
   the article. Do not paraphrase, do not fix typos, do not translate.

7. **When in doubt, say so.** Use `unsure` where the form offers it, and write a
   sentence in the *Annotator Notes*. A flagged uncertainty is useful to us; a
   confident guess is not.

# Step 1: Does this article describe a protest? {#sec-step1}

This is the only mandatory question on the form and it is asked at the level of the
**whole article**.

* **Yes / Possibly — code protest(s) below** — the article describes at least one
  protest event, or something that might be one.
* **No protest event described** — it does not.

## What we mean by a protest

> A **protest event** is a *public*, *collective* action by *non-state actors* that
> voices a grievance, a demand, or support for a cause, addressed to an audience or
> a target beyond the participants themselves.

All four elements have to be present:

| Element | Means | Fails when |
|----|--------|--------|
| **Collective** | More than one person acting together | A single person acting alone |
| **Public** | In public space, or publicly visible and directed at a public | A closed internal meeting, a private dispute |
| **Claim-making** | Expresses a demand, grievance, criticism or support | A crowd with no message: a concert, a festival, a football match |
| **An event** | Something that happened, is happening, or is announced for a specific date and place | A general mood, an attitude, an intention |

## Counts as a protest

Demonstration, Kundgebung, Protestmarsch, Demonstrationszug, Mahnwache, Vigil,
Menschenkette, Sitzblockade, Blockade, Besetzung, Protestcamp, Streik, Warnstreik,
Arbeitsniederlegung, Tarifstreik, Hungerstreik (collective), Straßenblockade,
Traktorenkorso and other Korso-Aktionen, Störaktion at a public event, Banner- and
Transparentaktion, Flashmob with a political message, Autokorso, Fahrraddemo,
Montagsspaziergang, Kirchenasyl-Aktion, publicly staged handover of a petition
with a gathering, riots that grow out of a demonstration, fan protests in or
around a stadium with banners or chants directed at a target.

Protests **anywhere in the world** count, not only in Germany. There is a country
field for exactly that reason.

## Does not count as a protest

* **Verbal or written objection without a gathering**: a politician who
  "protestiert gegen" something, a Protestnote, a Protestbrief, an open letter, a
  press statement, a party resolution, a legal Einspruch or Widerspruch, a
  complaint to a broadcaster.
* **Online-only activity**: a hashtag, a shitstorm, an online petition, a boycott
  call on social media with no physical action.
* **Elections and votes** described as protest: "Protestwahl", "Denkzettel für die
  Regierung", protest votes in a parliament.
* **Crowds without a claim**: concerts, festivals, Volksfeste, sporting events,
  Gedenkveranstaltungen and Trauerfeiern, religious processions, parades,
  celebrations, party conferences, press conferences, trade fairs.
* **Violence without a protest**: terror attacks, drone strikes, war reporting,
  riots between hooligans, looting, arson attacks, Anschläge. A military strike is
  not a protest, however loudly it is condemned.
* **State action**: police raids, evictions carried out by authorities, court
  decisions, deportations — unless people protest against them, in which case the
  protest is the event.
* **Passing mentions with no substance**: an article about pension reform that
  ends with "immer wieder gab es Proteste" and gives no event, no date, no place
  and no participants.

## Awkward cases and how to handle them

| Case | Decision |
|-------|----------|
| Article reports a protest **announced for next Saturday**, with place and date | Yes. Enter the announced date as the event date and add a note |
| A vague call to mobilize, no date, no place | Yes / Possibly, `is_protest = unsure`, plus a note |
| A **historical** protest (1989, 1968) reported as a feature | Yes / Possibly, code it, and add a note that the event is historical |
| A historical protest mentioned only as background | No |
| A **single person** chained to a fence, one lone hunger striker | Yes / Possibly, `is_protest = unsure` |
| **Booing and whistling** at a politician's speech | Yes / Possibly, `is_protest = unsure` |
| Fans display a banner against their club's management | Yes |
| A **strike** or Warnstreik | Yes — strikes are protests for this project |
| An **AfD or right-wing extremist** rally | Yes. Who protests is irrelevant to whether it is a protest |
| A **counter-demonstration** | Yes, but usually *not* as a separate protest — see @sec-units |
| A protest inside another country's parliament | Yes / Possibly, `unsure` — these are rarely non-state actors in public space |
| The article is a **commentary** about protests in general | No, unless a concrete event is described |

: Frequent borderline cases {tbl-colwidths="[55,45]"}

If you tick "No protest event described", you are done with the article. Submit.

# One protest, or several? {#sec-units}

This decision shapes everything that follows, and it is the one coders could easily 
disagree about. The unit of analysis is the **protest event**, not the article
and not the city.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule

Simultaneous actions by the **same organizers** about the **same issue** on the
**same date** are **one protest**, even if they take place in twelve different
cities. List all the cities in the *Locations* field.

Open a **new protest block** only when events differ in at least one of:
**date**, **organizing group**, or **central issue**.
:::

Worked through:

| Situation | How to code |
|--------|--------|
| Nationwide climate strike, Fridays for Future, 12 cities, one Friday | **One** protest, 12 lines in *Locations* |
| Same union strikes on Monday in Köln and on Wednesday in Bonn | **Two** protests (different dates) |
| A demonstration and a Gegendemo, same day, same place | **One** protest. The Gegendemo goes into the *Counter-Protestors* field, not into its own block |
| A protest camp that has lasted five days | **One** protest, *Number of Days* = 5 |
| A weekly Monday demo; the article reports on this week's | **One** protest — this week's |
| Two marches on the same day in Berlin, one against the AfD, one about rents | **Two** protests (different issues) |
| A "wave of protests" across the country with no concrete events described | Code the ones that have details; describe the rest in the notes |
| An article that reports on more than five distinct protests | Code the five that get the most attention in the article and describe the others in the notes |

When you genuinely cannot tell whether an article describes one event in several
places or several separate events, treat it as **one** protest and write a note.

# Coding a protest: the fields one by one

Everything below is repeated identically for Protest 1 to Protest 5. Only the
first block is described here.

## Is this a protest? (`is_protest`)

Repeats the Step 1 judgement for *this specific event*.

* **yes** — a clear demonstration, march, rally, strike, blockade or occupation.
* **unsure** — an ambiguous event: a disruption at a public meeting, a spontaneous
  gathering with no obvious protest character, a lone actor, a fan action, a crowd
  whose demand you cannot identify.

Both answers keep the protest in the data. `unsure` is a quality flag, not a
rejection.

## Event Date (`event_date`)

Format **YYYY-MM-DD**, e.g. `2024-09-20`. Derive it from the publication date shown
in the article panel plus the temporal expressions in the text.

| The article says (published Fri 2025-11-15) | Enter |
|--------|--------|
| "gestern" | 2025-11-14 |
| "am Donnerstag" (past tense) | 2025-11-13 |
| "heute" / "am Freitag" | 2025-11-15 |
| "am kommenden Samstag" | 2025-11-16 |
| "am Wochenende" (past tense) | 2025-11-09 — use the **Saturday** |
| "seit Montag" for an ongoing event | 2025-11-10 — the **first** day |
| "im vergangenen Sommer", no more detail | leave blank, add a note |

For a multi-day event, always enter the **first** day. If the date cannot be
derived at all, leave the field empty rather than guessing.

## Number of Days (`num_days`)

How many days the event lasts, as reported. `1` for an ordinary demonstration.
For an event that is still running when the article appears, enter the number of
days it has lasted **so far** according to the article, and add a note.

## Locations (`locations`)

One line per city, four fields separated by the pipe character `|`:

```
Venue | City | Bundesland | Country
```

Use a single hyphen `-` when a part is not given. Write the Bundesland out in full
and in German. For places outside Germany, use the region, state or province if the
article names one, `-` otherwise, and give the country in German.

```
Bahnhofsvorplatz | Köln | Nordrhein-Westfalen | Deutschland
Brandenburger Tor | Berlin | Berlin | Deutschland
- | Hamburg | Hamburg | Deutschland
Trafalgar Square | London | England | Vereinigtes Königreich
```

The venue is the specific square, street, building or institution the protest took
place at or in front of: *Bahnhofsvorplatz*, *Rathausmarkt*, *vor dem Kanzleramt*,
*Werkstor von VW*. Leave it as `-` if only the city is named.

List **every** city mentioned as a site of this protest, including those with no
further detail.

## Protest Size Estimates (`size_estimates`)

This is the single most important field in the study, and the one that most often
gets under-filled. The project estimates the *true* size of protests from the
disagreement between sources, so we need **every number, with its source, kept
apart from every other number**.

One line per estimate, five fields separated by `|`:

```
source_type | verbatim text | conservative number | source name or - | city or -
```

**`source_type`** is one of exactly these six values:

| Value | Use when the number comes from |
|-------|-------|
| `organizers` | The organizing group, Veranstalter, Anmelder, a union calling the strike |
| `police` | The police, Polizei, Polizeisprecher |
| `media` | The reporting outlet itself or another named news organization ("nach Zählung unseres Reporters") |
| `other` | A named third party: city administration, researchers, a counting initiative, a company |
| `unattributed` | No source at all: "Rund 2000 Menschen versammelten sich" |
| `unclear` | A source is implied but cannot be identified: "Beobachter sprachen von" |

**`verbatim text`** is the number exactly as printed, including German formatting
and vagueness: `15.000`, `rund 2000`, `Hunderte`, `mehr als zehntausend`.

**`conservative number`** turns that into a plain integer, always erring on the low
side:

| Wording | Number |
|-------|------|
| (ein paar / mehrere) Dutzend, Dutzende | 24 |
| Hunderte, mehrere Hundert | 200 |
| Tausende, mehrere Tausend | 2000 |
| Zehntausende | 20000 |
| Hunderttausende | 200000 |
| rund / etwa / ca. / knapp 2000 | 2000 |
| mehr als 2000 | 2000 |
| 2000 bis 3000 | 2000 (the lower bound) |
| eine dreistellige Zahl | 100 |
| no number given, only "viele" | leave the line out entirely |

**`source name`** names the concrete source where the article does: `Polizei Berlin`,
`Fridays for Future`, `ver.di`, `Stadt München`. Use `-` if it is not named.

**`city`** is the city this particular number refers to. Use `-` when the number
covers the whole event across all cities.

Example, for an article reporting a nationwide strike:

```
police | 15.000 | 15000 | Polizei Berlin | Berlin
organizers | 10.000 | 10000 | Fridays for Future | Hamburg
unattributed | Zehntausende | 20000 | - | -
```

Note what happened there: the police figure for Berlin, the organizers' figure for
Hamburg, and the overall figure are **three separate lines**. Never merge them,
never average them, and never drop a number because another one contradicts it.
The contradictions are our data.

## Main Issue (`main_issue`)

One short German phrase naming the central demand or grievance — not a summary of
the article and not a summary of the event.

* Good: `Klimagerechtigkeit und Einhaltung des Pariser Abkommens`
* Good: `Höhere Löhne im öffentlichen Dienst`
* Good: `Gegen die Abschiebung einer Familie aus Wuppertal`
* Bad: `Eine Demonstration in Köln mit 2000 Teilnehmern`

## Topics, Primary Topic and Citations

**Topics** is a multiple-choice list: tick every topic that the article makes
*clearly* relevant to this protest. Do not tick topics that are only implied or
tangential — if the connection needs an argument, leave it out.

**Which topic is primary?** Pick exactly one, the central issue of the protest. It
must be one of the topics you ticked above.

**Citations**: paste one or two verbatim sentences from the article that justify
your choice.

| Topic | Covers |
|-----|------|
| Climate & Environment | Climate policy, emissions, coal and lignite, forests, pollution, nature and animal protection, transport policy when framed ecologically |
| Social Justice | General fairness and solidarity demands, poverty, welfare benefits, pensions, when not primarily about wages |
| Racism / Discrimination | Racism, antisemitism, anti-Muslim racism, hostility to Roma and Sinti, discrimination against minorities or disabled people |
| Anti-Right-Wing Extremism | Protests *against* the far right: "Demo gegen Rechts", against the AfD, against neo-Nazi marches |
| Right-Wing Extremism | Protests organized *by* far-right actors: neo-Nazi marches, Pegida, far-right rallies |
| Gender / Feminism | Women's rights, gender equality, abortion, sexualized violence, equal pay |
| LGBTQ+ Rights | Queer rights, CSD and Pride, trans rights, and mobilization against them |
| Immigration / Asylum | Refugees, deportations, migration policy — both restrictive and welcoming positions |
| War / Peace | Wars and armed conflicts, arms deliveries, Ukraine, Israel and Gaza, Bundeswehr, conscription, peace demonstrations |
| Economic Inequality | Distribution of wealth, taxation of the rich, cost of living, inflation, subsidies |
| Labor / Workers' Rights | Strikes, Tarifrunden, wages, working conditions, layoffs, plant closures |
| Housing | Rents, evictions, housing shortage, Mietendeckel, squatting |
| Education | Schools, universities, tuition, teacher shortage, education funding |
| Healthcare | Hospitals and clinic closures, Pflege, health insurance, medical supply |
| Digital / Privacy | Surveillance, data protection, Chatkontrolle, AI regulation, net policy |
| EU Politics | EU-level policy and institutions, EU accession, European elections |
| Energy Policy | Energy prices, nuclear power, wind and solar infrastructure, Heizungsgesetz, pipelines — where the framing is supply and price rather than climate |
| COVID / Health Policy | Pandemic measures, vaccination mandates, Querdenken |
| East-West Issues | East–West German inequality, grievances specific to Ostdeutschland |
| Other | Anything genuinely not covered above. Use sparingly and make the Main Issue precise |

: The twenty topics

Recurring German cases, so that we all treat them the same way:

* **Bauernproteste** against subsidy and diesel-tax cuts → primary
  *Economic Inequality*; add *Climate & Environment* only if the article frames it
  that way.
* **Tarifrunde im ÖPNV** → primary *Labor / Workers' Rights*; add
  *Climate & Environment* when the article mentions a climate alliance.
* **Demo gegen Rechts** after a far-right scandal → primary
  *Anti-Right-Wing Extremism*; *Racism / Discrimination* often secondary.
* **Pro-Palestinian or pro-Israel demonstrations** → primary *War / Peace*;
  *Racism / Discrimination* secondary if antisemitism or anti-Muslim racism is a
  theme in the article.
* **Anti-windfarm protests by local residents** → primary *Energy Policy*.

## Protest Slogan (`slogan`)

The motto of the protest as printed: `"Wir sind die Brandmauer"`,
`"Nie wieder ist jetzt"`, `"Hände weg vom Wedding"`. Leave the field **blank** if
the article does not quote one. The name of the organizing group is not a slogan.

## Target (`target`)

Who or what the protest is directed at, in German: `Bundesregierung`, `AfD`,
`Landesregierung Sachsen`, `Deutsche Bahn`, `Tesla`, `Israelische Regierung`,
`Heizungsgesetz`. For a protest *in favour of* something, name the addressee of the
demand. Leave blank if the article gives you no target.

## Organizing Groups (`organizations`)

One per line, named as the article names them. Include groups described as having
called for the protest ("hatte zu der Demonstration aufgerufen") and members of a
named alliance. Do not include parties or organizations that are merely mentioned
in passing, and do not include the target. Leave blank if no organizer is named.

```
Fridays for Future
ver.di
Bündnis "Zusammen gegen Rechts"
```

## Participant Demographics (`demographics`)

Groups the article explicitly describes among the participants, one per line, in
German: `Studierende`, `Landwirte`, `Beschäftigte der Charité`,
`Familien mit Kindern`, `Rentnerinnen und Rentner`, `Schülerinnen und Schüler`.

Only what is stated. That a union organized the strike does not license
`Gewerkschaftsmitglieder`. If the article says nothing, leave it blank.

## Counter-Protestors

**Reported? Yes / No.** Yes if the article reports an opposing gathering,
Gegendemo, or Gegenkundgebung connected to this protest, including hecklers
described as an organized counter-presence. In the details box: who they were and
how many, as far as the article says.

Remember: a counter-demonstration belongs **here**, not in its own protest block.

## Police

The only three-way field on the form.

* **Present** — police are described as being at the event in any capacity:
  securing it, escorting the march, standing by, intervening, being attacked. By
  convention we also code **Present** when the article quotes the police *about
  this event* ("laut Polizei kamen 15.000"), since that implies officers on site.
* **Not present** — the article states that no police were there, or that police
  stayed away.
* **Not reported** — the article does not mention the police at all. This is the
  most common answer.

The details box takes anything **beyond mere presence**: Absperrungen,
Platzverweise, Ingewahrsamnahmen, Räumung, Wasserwerfer, Pfefferspray,
Schlagstockeinsatz, Kessel — and any police violence the article describes.

## Arrests

**Reported? Yes / No**, plus the number. *Festnahmen*, *vorläufige Festnahmen* and
*Ingewahrsamnahmen* all count. Enter the figure if the article gives one, or
`unknown` if arrests are reported without a number.

## Protester Violence

**Reported? Yes / No**, plus a type code if yes. Violence carried out **by
protesters** — not violence against them.

The three components:

* **Weapons** — weapons or objects used as weapons against people: Messer,
  Schusswaffen, Steine, Flaschen, Feuerwerkskörper, Pyrotechnik.
* **Physical** — bodily force against people without weapons: Schläge, Tritte,
  Rangeleien, Durchbrechen einer Polizeikette, Widerstand gegen Festnahmen.
* **Other** — other violent acts: Brandstiftung, Vandalismus, throwing objects at
  buildings or vehicles rather than at people.

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 | Weapons only |
| 2 | Physical assault only |
| 3 | Other violence only |
| 4 | Weapons + Physical |
| 5 | Weapons + Other |
| 6 | Physical + Other |
| 7 | Weapons + Physical + Other |

A peaceful blockade or a sit-in is **not** violence, even where it is illegal.
Shouting, insults and provocation are **not** violence. If the article says the
protest was "weitgehend friedlich" but reports isolated incidents, the answer is
still **Yes**.

## Property Damage

**Reported? Yes / No**, plus the amount in euros or `unknown`. Broken windows,
graffiti, damaged cars, damaged police vehicles, destroyed fences, damage to a
building being occupied.

## Injuries

Four separate questions — **Protesters**, **Bystanders**, **Police**, **Others** —
each Yes / No plus a number. Enter `unknown` when injuries are reported without a
figure. For *Others*, also fill the "who" box: `Journalisten`, `Sanitäter`,
`Ordner`.

Remember rule 3: if the article says nothing about injuries, all four are **No**.

## Deaths

Structured exactly like Injuries, for deaths. Almost always four times **No**.

## Sentiment

How the **article frames** this protest. Not your own view of the protest, not the
mood among the participants, not the tone of the quotes.

* **Positive (sympathetic)** — the reporting is on the side of the protest: the
  demands are presented as legitimate, the size and peacefulness are stressed,
  protesters speak and critics do not, descriptive language is warm.
* **Neutral (factual)** — plain reporting: what happened, where, how many, who
  said what, both sides quoted, no evaluative language.
* **Negative (dismissive/threatening)** — the protest is framed as a problem: the
  emphasis is on disruption, chaos, violence, extremism or radicalism, the
  protesters are portrayed as a fringe or a danger, critics dominate the quotes,
  the demands are treated as unreasonable.

Most news articles are **neutral**. Reserve positive and negative for a clear tilt
you could point at in the text. Commentaries and opinion pieces are the usual place
where a tilt is unmistakable.

## Keywords

Three to seven comma-separated German keywords for search on the dashboard:
movement, issue, place, main actors.

```
Klimastreik, Fridays for Future, Berlin, Pariser Abkommen
```

# Adding further protests {#sec-more}

Beneath Protest 1 there is a dashed box with a checkbox:

> **+ This article contains a second distinct protest event**

Tick it and the Protest 2 block appears, in a different colour, with exactly the
same fields. The same pattern repeats up to **Protest 5**.

Before ticking, re-read @sec-units — most articles that look like several protests
are one protest in several cities.

::: {.callout-warning}
If you tick the box by mistake, **clear the fields you already filled in the block
before you untick it**. Hiding a block does not necessarily delete what you entered
in it.
:::

For an article with more than five distinct protests, code the five that the
article treats most fully and describe the rest in the notes.

# Annotator Notes

The purple box at the bottom is always available and always optional. Use it for:

* uncertainties and how you resolved them;
* the flags this codebook asks for: announced future events, historical events,
  ambiguous one-vs-several decisions, truncated text;
* more than five protests in one article;
* anything about the article that the form cannot express;
* cases where you think the coding scheme itself is wrong.

Write in German or English, whichever is faster for you. One sentence is enough.

# Two worked examples

## Example 1 — a single-city protest

**Article** (published 2025-11-15), headline *Klimademo in Köln*:

> Gestern veranstaltete "Fridays for Future" in Köln eine Laternendemo am
> Bahnhofsvorplatz. Rund 2000 Menschen, darunter primär Studierende, erschienen
> laut Angaben der Organisator:innen. Sie protestieren für Klimagerechtigkeit und
> fordern eine Einhaltung des Pariser Abkommens von der Bundesregierung.

| Field | Entry |
|-----|-------|
| Step 1 | Yes / Possibly |
| Is this a protest? | yes |
| Event Date | 2025-11-14 (published 15th, "gestern") |
| Number of Days | 1 |
| Locations | Bahnhofsvorplatz \| Köln \| Nordrhein-Westfalen \| Deutschland |
| Size Estimates | organizers \| rund 2000 \| 2000 \| Fridays for Future \| - |
| Main Issue | Klimagerechtigkeit und Einhaltung des Pariser Abkommens |
| Topics | Climate & Environment |
| Primary Topic | Climate & Environment |
| Citations | "Sie protestieren für Klimagerechtigkeit und fordern eine Einhaltung des Pariser Abkommens" |
| Slogan | *(blank — none quoted)* |
| Target | Bundesregierung |
| Organizations | Fridays for Future |
| Demographics | Studierende |
| Counter-Protestors | No |
| Police | Not reported |
| Arrests | No |
| Protester Violence | No |
| Property Damage | No |
| Injuries | No / No / No / No |
| Deaths | No / No / No / No |
| Sentiment | Neutral |
| Keywords | Klimagerechtigkeit, Fridays for Future, Laternendemo, Köln, Pariser Abkommen |

Note that the size estimate has no city: it refers to the whole event, which only
took place in one city anyway.

## Example 2 — one protest across several cities

**Article** (published 2024-09-21), headline *Bundesweiter Klimastreik*:

> Am gestrigen Freitag gingen bundesweit Zehntausende auf die Straße. In Berlin
> versammelten sich laut Polizei 15.000 Menschen am Brandenburger Tor, in Hamburg
> zählten die Veranstalter 10.000 Teilnehmer. In München fand ebenfalls eine
> Kundgebung statt. Organisiert wurde der Streik von "Fridays for Future". In
> Berlin kam es vereinzelt zu Auseinandersetzungen mit der Polizei.

This is **one** protest: one organizer, one issue, one date. Three cities go into
*Locations*:

```
Brandenburger Tor | Berlin | Berlin | Deutschland
- | Hamburg | Hamburg | Deutschland
- | München | Bayern | Deutschland
```

and three separate numbers go into *Size Estimates*:

```
police | 15.000 | 15000 | Polizei Berlin | Berlin
organizers | 10.000 | 10000 | Fridays for Future | Hamburg
unattributed | Zehntausende | 20000 | - | -
```

The rest of the form:

| Field | Entry |
|-----|-------|
| Step 1 | Yes / Possibly |
| Is this a protest? | yes |
| Event Date | 2024-09-20 |
| Number of Days | 1 |
| Locations | the three lines above |
| Size Estimates | the three lines above |
| Main Issue | Klimaschutz |
| Topics / Primary | Climate & Environment |
| Citations | "Bundesweiter Klimastreik" |
| Slogan | *(blank)* |
| Target | *(blank — none named)* |
| Organizations | Fridays for Future |
| Demographics | *(blank)* |
| Counter-Protestors | No |
| Police | **Present** — details: "vereinzelt zu Auseinandersetzungen mit der Polizei" in Berlin |
| Arrests | No |
| Protester Violence | No — "Auseinandersetzungen" alone is too vague to code as violence by protesters; add a note |
| Property Damage | No |
| Injuries / Deaths | No throughout |
| Sentiment | Neutral |
| Keywords | Klimastreik, Fridays for Future, Berlin, Hamburg, München |

Note the München line: a city named as a site of the protest is listed even though
the article gives no venue and no number for it.

# Before you submit — checklist

* [ ] Step 1 answered.
* [ ] Every free-text box **added** with Shift + Enter or the *Add* button, and the
      text visible as an entry below the box.
* [ ] Every yes/no block answered — counter-protestors, police, arrests, protester
      violence, property damage, four injuries, four deaths.
* [ ] Sentiment set.
* [ ] Every number in the article that refers to crowd size is on its own line in
      *Size Estimates*, with its source.
* [ ] Every city named as a site of the protest is in *Locations*.
* [ ] Exactly one primary topic, and it is among the ticked topics.
* [ ] One protest block per genuinely distinct event — no block opened for a
      counter-demo or for a second city.
* [ ] A note written for anything you were unsure about.

# Frequently asked questions

**The article describes a protest but gives almost no detail. Do I still code it?**
Yes. Answer Step 1 with "Yes / Possibly", fill what is there, leave the rest blank,
and answer all the yes/no questions with No.

**I disagree with the sentiment of an article but cannot point to a passage.**
Then it is neutral. Sentiment must be defensible from the text.

**The article contradicts itself about a number.**
Enter both numbers as separate lines in *Size Estimates* with their sources, and
note the contradiction.

**The protest is abroad and I do not know the region.**
Put `-` in the Bundesland position and the country in German.

**The article is in a language other than German.**
If you can read it, code it. If not, note it and Skip.

**Am I supposed to be fast?**
No. Every article you code carefully is worth several coded quickly. If you are
consistently unsure about a rule, that is worth reporting — it means the codebook
needs fixing, and fixing it is part of the point of this exercise.

**Something in the interface behaves oddly.**
Note the article ID from the bottom left of the screen and report it. Do not try to
work around it silently.
